data.title: How the NATO phonetic alphabet works
data.text:
The NATO phonetic alphabet, formally the International Radiotelephony Spelling Alphabet (also called the ICAO spelling alphabet or military alphabet), gives every letter a distinct code word: A is Alfa, B is Bravo, C is Charlie. These words are designed to remain recognisable over radio static, weak phone calls and language differences, so they are used to spell names, call signs, registration numbers, passwords and short codes aloud.

Enter ordinary text to convert it into code words, or switch to decode mode to turn a spoken or written sequence such as Charlie Alfa Tango back into CAT. The translator recognises the official forms and common alternatives such as Alpha, Juliet, Xray and Whisky. Spaces between original words are shown as /, making long names and identifiers easier to read.

Choose the spelling system that fits your situation: standard NATO/ICAO; Aviation for radio number words such as Tree, Fower, Fife and Niner; the older US police/LAPD set, including Adam, Boy, Charles; or the German DIN 5009 alphabet, including Anton, Berta, Cäsar. You can separate code words with spaces, hyphens, commas or line breaks, and display them either as words alone or as pairs such as A = Alfa.

In encode mode, select Listen to hear the generated words with your browser’s built-in speech synthesis and adjust the reading speed if needed. The conversion and audio are handled locally in your browser; no text needs to be sent to a server.

data.question: Is it Alfa or Alpha, Juliett or Juliet?
data.answer: The official ICAO/NATO spellings are Alfa and Juliett — with an F and a double T — so that speakers of any language pronounce them correctly. The common English spellings Alpha and Juliet mean the same letters; this tool outputs the official forms but accepts both when decoding.

data.question: Why do pilots say Niner, Fife and Tree?
data.answer: In aviation and military radio, several digits are altered so they cannot be confused: nine becomes “niner” (to avoid the German “nein”), five becomes “fife” and three becomes “tree”. Select the Aviation variant to use these number words.

data.question: Can I hear how the words are pronounced?
data.answer: Yes. In encode mode press the Listen button and your browser will read the code words aloud using its built-in speech synthesis. You can also adjust the reading speed. No audio is sent anywhere — it is generated on your device.

data.question: Is the NATO phonetic alphabet the same as the ICAO alphabet?
data.answer: Yes. The official system is called the International Radiotelephony Spelling Alphabet and is used by both NATO and the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). In everyday use it is commonly called the NATO alphabet, ICAO alphabet or aviation spelling alphabet.

data.question: How do I format the translated code words?
data.answer: Choose spaces, hyphens, commas or line breaks as the separator. You can also show code words alone, such as “Alfa Bravo”, or include the matching character, such as “A = Alfa, B = Bravo”. A slash marks the boundary between words in the original text.

data.question: What happens to punctuation or unsupported characters?
data.answer: The encoder converts letters and digits that belong to the selected spelling alphabet and skips other characters, including punctuation. If an unrecognised token appears while decoding, the result shows a question mark, so you can spot and correct it.
